To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
reading of words and pseudoword are associated with different brain structures and reading speed correlates with activation onset in these brain structures.

the brain regions that subserve phonological analysis of print during reading are different for words and pseudoword and that the time course of brain activity is different for the two types of stimuli.

(i) there are two distinct neural pathways for reading words, one that is involved in the processing of exception words and another that is involved in reading pseudowords; (ii) reading of meaningful words is associated with greater activation of the left middle temporal gyrus, whereas reading of pseudowords is associated with much reduced activity of the middle temporal gyrus; and (iii) the onset of activity of the left posterior MTGp correlates with the pronunciation latencies of exception words
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms of reading and the way in which they support the development of reading skills.
the brain structures involved when reading words and pseudohomophonic and pseudoword strings.

the neural correlates of two different types of reading processes: (i) the process of assembling the phonological form of a printed word, and (ii) the process of accessing the phonological form from the mental lexicon.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no one single mechanism for reading words and that the brain regions involved in reading words depend on the type of print and the reading strategy.
the brain mechanisms for reading pseudohomophonic words and exception words are different and that these mechanisms are not the same as those for reading pseudowords.

there are at least two brain mechanisms for reading words, and that the brain structures supporting these mechanisms differ from each other in terms of both anatomical location and functional specialization.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are two distinct brain mechanisms for reading words: one that is involved in the processing of assembled phonology and one that is responsible for the addressed phonology.

the posterior middle temporal lobe is involved in the processing of words with rare print-to-sound correspondences, whereas the posterior STGp is involved in the assembly of the phonological code for words with regular print-to-sound correspondence and pseudowords.
the brain mechanisms involved in reading words and non-words are different.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the brain structures that subserve the phonological processes of word reading are different and that the posterior middle temporal gyruses is the main brain area that subserves the addressed phonological mechanism.

reading of meaningful and meaningless letter strings is mediated by different neural networks, and that the neural networks involved in reading of meaningful items are not simply a more elaborated version of those that are involved in the reading of meaningless letter string.
the neural systems that support phonological reading are not the same for all types of print, and that they are differentially engaged
